chapter: Lester Nelson and New Orleans players
title: Les Nelson, fisherman and tenor player
summary: Les Nelson's lure-making, his playing like Eddie Miller, and his death; Charlie DuPont and Ronnie DuPont, Jimmy LaRocca.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: door open. Gosh, when was that? And that was when Gene Austin heard these guys and picked
them up. Well, we can figure that out. We can figure the date out on that. Yeah, and
I don't think Monk was not playing with us, because the first time I ever played with Monk was in Sharky's band. But Coco and Candy and I. We were going to talk about Les Nelson.
All those fishing rods reminded me of him. You're talking about flies. I know he must have

loved to fish. Les Nelson made the most beautiful. He was internationally famous for making lures, especially flies, for fly casting for bass. And he could make, he could carve a wooden lure that looked to you like it was alive. And he specialized in making ear rings with small fish. And they sold all over the world. Boy, he was an artist. Absolutely played fine tenor sax. And one of the most somber persons that you ever met in all of your life. Very seldom, if ever, laughed. That seems unusual for Dad's musicians. But he was not cranky or anything like that. He was just dry. And a marvelous personality. And Butts Massico that was here just before you all came. I told them you were coming. And Butts and Lester bummed together all the time, because they both were such fine bass fishermen. And they hunted ducks together and all. What killed Lester Nelson was not dissipation with liquor, but lack of taking care of his own well-being, his body. He would go and hunt all day long without food, you know. One of those kinds of things. He was not a boozer. I know. I know. You told me that he had a lot of transfusions.

The fast as they put the blood in him, it poured out of him. It was pitiful. And Charlie DuPont and I, Charlie DuPont can tell you. Mm-hmm. Now Charlie DuPont and I played together on and off since 1927. That's Ronnie's daddy. Yeah, I know him. He played my wedding. So Ronnie not long ago and called me Unk. I held him in my arms. That's Al H. I was a great pianist. Ronnie DuPont. I held him in my arms when he was a baby and took him in my arms the other night. He was playing with Jimmy Ile. I think that he will be back with hate before long.
Well, he's so good to me that I don't care who he's playing with, he's still Ronnie.

He really plays nice solos, and I wish I could hear more of it. And he's just as sweet a guy as you ever met in your life. I used to hear him some with Connie in a trio. Connie Jones just had a little trio, and sometimes he'd use Harvey Rubin, and different piano players.
One of them was, oh, you know, Armand's brother-in-law, Armand Hugg's brother. Bob Doyle.
Bob Doyle, he had a variety of piano players.

Bob Doyle was a fine piano man. I had a mighty nice thing happen to me, this last jazz thing that they had, right across the street from Sheraton, the Sheraton Canal. And they were calling on different piano players to play, and there was three or four piano players that asked Jimmy LaRocca, and I happened to be one of them, and they said, well, what piano player do you want? He said, I don't want anybody but Jeff. That was mighty sweet. And he always, when I play with him, comes up while we're playing, and while I'm taking my solo, he walks around and takes and kisses me on the cheek in front of everybody. I just think that's marvelous. Don't you?
And I'm old enough to be his father.

You know, I think there's so many wonderful players here that have been neglected like that, too. I don't think Ronnie's ever gotten his due, and I certainly think Leslie Nelson must have been marvelous. I just wish I could have heard him once to know what he sounded like.
He had a beautiful style and got a beautiful tone out of the morning, out of a tenor. Uh-huh. And just as dry as a boy.
Did he sound at all like anybody that I'd know?
Oh, yes. Very much, very much like him. You want to know who? Yes. Miller. Got a tone like Eddie Miller and played a style like Eddie Miller.
